body:
The right goal is therefore **positive expected value, applied repeatedly, with survival guaranteed**. Expected value is the probability of a win times the size of the win, minus the probability of a loss times the size of the loss. Howard Marks's "second-level thinking" asks you to set out the range of likely outcomes, the probability that you are right, what consensus believes and what the price implies ([Oaktree, "It's Not Easy"](https://www.advisorperspectives.com/commentaries/2015/09/24/it-s-not-easy)). Druckenmiller, crediting Soros, says what matters is "how much you make when you're right and how much you lose when you're wrong," not your hit rate ([MoneyWeek](https://moneyweek.com/investments/investment-strategy/605020/stan-druckenmiller-position-size-really-matters)). Pabrai's version is "Heads I win; tails I don't lose much" ([Outlook Money](https://www.outlookmoney.com/invest/mohnish-pabrais-lessons-in-the-dhandho-of-investing)). If 2–4% of stocks create all the wealth, a multibagger portfolio has to be judged on whether **a few large winners pay for many small losers**, not on how often you are right. The playbook below is built around that idea.

| "Certainty" framing (wrong) | Probabilistic reframing (right) |
|---|---|
| "This stock will 10x" | "I estimate a 20% chance of 10x, 50% of roughly flat, 30% of −50%. EV is positive and the downside is survivable." |
| "I'm confident, so I'll go big" | "Size from the downside and from estimation error. Cap any one position." |
| "It fell 30%, so the thesis is wrong" or "...so I'll buy more" | "Did a pre-written kill criterion trigger? If not, price alone is not information about the thesis." |
| "My win rate is 70%" | "My average win divided by my average loss, times my hit rate, is my expectancy, measured over 30+ decisions." |
| "The AI said buy" | "The AI produced a hypothesis. I verified the numbers against the source and red-teamed it." |

---

body:
`person:group-ruchi-patanjali` · flag: **poor (Shahra); mixed (Patanjali)** · confidence: verified · tickers: PATANJALI

Flag: POOR (Shahra era) / MIXED (Patanjali era). Ruchi Soya, an edible-oil major run by the Shahra family, over-borrowed and lost money on commodity bets and was admitted to IBC (Dec-2017; ~Rs 12,000 cr debt). Patanjali Ayurved won with a ~Rs 4,350 cr plan (2019); after relisting in Jan-2020 only ~1.1% of shares were public, and the stock rose from ~Rs 17 to over Rs 1,500 within months -- a thin-float price not reflecting fundamentals (market cap briefly exceeding many FMCG majors). The Mar-2022 FPO (Rs 4,300 cr) saw SEBI ask the company to let investors withdraw bids after unsolicited SMS messages promoting the issue circulated. Public float stayed below 25% (19.18% after FPO), so NSE/BSE froze 29.25 cr promoter shares (80.82% of equity) in Mar-2023 for MPS non-compliance; Patanjali Ayurved sold ~2.53 cr shares by OFS (Jul-2024) to reach 73.82% promoter holding. Renamed Patanjali Foods; absorbed Patanjali Ayurved's food business (2022, Rs 690 cr) and later its home & personal care business -- related-party acquisitions from the promoter that need independent valuation scrutiny. Patanjali Ayurved separately faced Supreme Court contempt proceedings over misleading ads (2024). Status Nov-2026: MPS compliant; watch further RPT acquisitions from the unlisted Patanjali Ayurved and the pricing of those deals.

- **red flags:** thin float post-IBC; FPO SMS episode; MPS freeze; RPT business transfers from promoter
- **good conduct:** MPS met via OFS 2024

**Calibration note.** These thresholds are practitioner conventions, assembled from Beneish, Sloan, Piotroski, Altman and Marcellus-style screens. They have **not yet been back-tested on Indian data by us.** Logging each scored company in memdb and checking the scores against outcomes 2–3 years later is how this becomes edge rather than ritual. That tracking task is in `next_steps`.

body: **False alarm: Costco's ~3% margin at 50-60x earnings** (`case_study:false-alarm-costco-thin-margins-high-pe`, verified). FLAGS: net margin only ~2.5-3% [approx, unverified]; gross markup capped at ~14-15%; P/E ~48-60x in 2024-26, a record. CONTEXT: the low margin is a deliberate strategy: low prices build trust and volume, and most operating profit comes from membership fees (~90% renewal in US/Canada), which are recurring, prepaid and rise every ~5-6 years without churn. Inventory turns fast, so suppliers effectively fund inventory (negative working capital), and ROIC is high despite thin margins. EPS ~$2.5 (FY09) -> ~$18 (FY25), ~7x, plus special dividends; stock ~$38 (2009) -> $1,094 (May 2026), ~29x. Charlie Munger (director from 1997) was the long-term advocate; Berkshire sold ~2020 near ~$300 and missed ~3.5x. HONEST CAVEAT: ~3.5x of the 29x came from P/E expansion (15 -> ~50x), which cannot repeat; the last time P/E was this high (1999, 56x) the stock fell >20% within months. LESSON: margin is a strategy choice; judge by ROIC, renewal rates and the source of profit. High P/E for certainty is benign for the business but a real risk for forward returns.
